title: Longest Absolute File Path
summary: A string describes an abstract filesystem: actual newline characters (\n) separate entries, and each leading tab (\t) increases the directory depth by one.
statement: A string describes an abstract filesystem: actual newline characters (\n) separate entries, and each leading tab (\t) increases the directory depth by one. Return the length of the longest absolute path to a file, including / separators, or 0 if there are no files. A dot distinguishes a filename from a directory name. Spaces inside names count. Process the supplied string only; do not inspect files on disk.
constraints: 1 <= input.length <= 10,000; the filesystem representation is valid.
Newline (\n) separates entries; leading tabs (\t) give directory depth. Spaces inside names count.
Directories contain letters/digits/spaces. A file has a nonempty name and extension separated by a dot.
Return the longest full file-path length including / separators, or 0 when there are no files. Do not access the real filesystem.
hints: A file path consists of its name plus its ancestor directory names and slashes.
Keep the cumulative prefix length for each directory depth, discarding deeper prefixes when moving to a sibling.
For depth d: total = prefix[d] + len(name). Update the answer for files; save total+1 as the child prefix for directories.
Only leading tabs encode depth. Do not strip spaces from names, and never let a long empty directory win.
editorial: Scan entries in their encoded preorder. Maintain directory-prefix lengths indexed by depth, starting with zero for root entries. A file updates the maximum; a directory stores its prefix including one slash for descendants. Trim stale deeper prefixes when the depth decreases. This operates only on a string, not files on disk. Splitting lines uses O(m) space in this implementation.

tests.explanation: The only file is dir/subdir2/file.ext: 3 + 1 + 7 + 1 + 8 = 20 characters.
The long directory branch has no file. Only the root file a.txt counts, so return 5.
